prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to systematic uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B061 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange sharpened my reasons. The chair asks which criterion should decide between B061 and B013, and I think the committee should state it plainly: the prize goes to a discovery or invention that is sharply defined, independently reproduced, and creditable to named people without distortion; breadth of follow-on physics is a legitimate tie-breaker but cannot substitute for those three conditions. On that test the lattice clock is the more complete case. The physics is atomic structure that can be checked line by line. The magic wavelength is where the differential polarisability of the two clock states vanishes to first order, so the lattice confines the atoms without shifting the transition. The blackbody-radiation shift, the dominant systematic, is set by the static polarisability difference and a small dynamic correction, and its control is what makes a 10^-18 uncertainty budget credible. Both steps have been reproduced in several independent laboratories and compared across institutes, so the claim is not open to reinterpretation. The two-name credit follows the logic of the work: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group then took the architecture to its limiting accuracy and stability and into the many-body regime. I would draw the citation narrowly on the neutral-atom optical lattice clock, with no statement about ion-clock priority or about who first reached any single milestone, which answers the chair's first question.
statement.case_against: I take three objections seriously and none has gone away. First, overlap: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems sit beside this result, so a sceptic can call it a successor refinement of a measurement we already knew how to make. I read the earlier citations as covering the comb and single-ion control, not the neutral-atom lattice clock, but the framing risk is real and I do not claim the matter is closed. Second, credit: Takamoto (Katori's group), Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Ludlow, PTB and NIST all contributed to demonstrations and comparisons, and a two-name prize leaves out people whose work was substantial. Third, timing: the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the practical culmination is still ahead. Against B013, I must also admit that on novelty of the regime opened, magic-angle graphene is plausibly the larger discovery, and a committee that weights that criterion first could reasonably order the two the other way.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B013 first as a prediction followed by an observation that nature supplied, and argues that ease of attribution should not decide the ranking over the opening of a new regime of correlated matter.
responses.response: I agree that attribution convenience should not by itself decide the ranking, and I have not argued that it should; it is a necessary condition for a prize we can write down, not a measure of importance. The point where we still differ is the criterion. If the prize rewarded the size of the field opened, B013 would lead. I put weight on a result that is complete as well as large. For the lattice clock the claim is fully specified and reproduced. For magic-angle graphene the existence of flat bands and correlated states is secure, but the mechanism of the superconductivity and the character of several correlated phases are still being debated, and the experimental credit leaves out Cao and Fatemi. You and Eriksson say the pairing mechanism is a wording issue only. I accept that for validity, but it means the citation would have to describe a platform rather than an explained phenomenon. I still treat B013 as my first alternative and would not obstruct it if the committee prefers breadth.

responses.point: Mehlig now prefers B013 and rates B061 as the more finished result, but argues the clocks are a precision refinement of an already honoured tradition while moire matter is a new regime of nature.
responses.response: Your concession that B061 is the more finished result is close to my whole argument, so I think we differ on one point, which is whether a clock is a refinement. A refinement improves a measurement already made with a known method. The lattice clock changed the method: it traps a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a light field tuned so that the clock transition is unperturbed, which removes the Doppler and recoil limits that constrain single-ion and fountain clocks. It also introduced new physics into the metrology, namely lattice light shifts, atomic collisions and many-body effects at the 10^-18 level. That is why I do not accept that 2005 and 2012 already honoured it. I do accept that this is a judgement about framing, and your weighting of novelty is a coherent alternative to mine. I would ask you to note that the credit objection to B013 that you raise yourself, and your wish to keep Bistritzer, make the three-name B013 set harder, not easier, to defend than the two-name B061 set.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the open pairing mechanism does not undermine B013, that the omissions cannot be repaired inside a three-name cap and should be acknowledged openly in the citation, and that Bistritzer should be kept.
responses.response: I accept your reading of maturity: the flat-band platform and the correlated phases are secure, and I do not hold the pairing mechanism against the validity of the discovery. I also agree that the committee should be open about omissions, and the same standard should apply to B061. If we choose clocks, we should say that the lattice-clock community extends beyond the two laureates, which is a drafting matter. Where I disagree is on how much weight can be placed on a statement of omissions. For B013 it would concern the first authors of the decisive experiments and earlier theory, which is a larger gap than the secondary groups in the clock field, because the clock claim of 10^-18 performance was demonstrated in Ye's own laboratory and independently confirmed, whereas the first authors of the 2018 experiments are outside the credited names. I would not remove Bistritzer from B013 to fit a pair, and I agree with Mehlig on that.

responses.point: Olsson asked me, as the atomic physicist, how to treat Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow and whether the 10^-18 milestones belong to Ye alone or to a wider group.
responses.response: As I recall the record, which I have not rechecked against sources here, the answer is a wider group working in a clear order. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice, and the first lattice-clock measurements came from his group in Tokyo, including Takamoto, and from Ye's group, with the SYRTE group of Lemonde and collaborators making early strontium and mercury lattice-clock measurements and comparisons. The 10^-18 systematic budgets and the stability that went with them were produced in Ye's laboratory, with graduate students and postdocs such as Ludlow doing much of the work. That separates a concept, a first demonstration and a limiting-performance programme. I think two names are defensible for the concept-plus-limiting-performance logic, but not free of cost, and a written citation that does not say first or only reduces the risk. I do not see a case for a third name, since neither Lemonde nor any other single figure owns a step that is separate from these two. I would be more worried if the committee tried to write a citation claiming the 10^-18 milestone for one person.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not already cover the lattice clock; I think they do not, but a colleague who weights precedent more heavily could reasonably disagree.

Whether recognition should wait for the redefinition of the second; I read the demonstrated performance and the cross-laboratory comparisons as sufficient, but the timing argument is a judgement and not a fact.

Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and other groups have claims that a two-name credit cannot honour; my account of the sequence of milestones is from memory and I have not verified it against sources.

Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism in B013 should weigh against it; I treat it as bearing on citation wording, not validity, but I recognise that I am weighing completeness more than novelty and that Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig weigh the criteria the other way.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I work in a neighbouring area of atomic structure and precision theory, and my documented collaborators (L'Huillier, Keller, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) are not credited names for B061, B013 or B034. I note the same general field proximity to B061, B034 and B005, and I continue to ask that Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory lineage be recorded, as Pearce also asks, while observing that my own ranking was reached on the atomic physics and not through that lineage. No recusal is proposed.
